first.rationale: Competitive pressure on price-sensitive SMB segment is immediate and directly addressable through promotional pricing (memory_73 shows strong acquisition lift). Verifying memory_86 (onboarding completion mechanics) and memory_73 (pricing effectiveness) is critical because onboarding decline (4% QoQ) may be correlated with acquisition source shifts if pricing pressure drives segment mix change—a factor that affects whether promotional pricing compounds the problem or solves it. Memory_31 and memory_91 together suggest activation gains are possible through messaging and friction reduction, but those are secondary responses to the immediate competitive threat. A small_guarded_test on promotional pricing for price-sensitive SMB cohorts allows us to (1) test whether pricing lifts acquisition enough to offset competitor pressure while (2) monitoring whether it cannibalizes enterprise or reference-ability, and (3) preserving capacity to pivot to activation_messaging if the pricing play fails. Referral incentives (memory_57) are longer-cycle and require existing customer base as lever. Enterprise sales assist (memory_44) is orthogonal to the current SMB compression. Risk flagged: promotional pricing may establish price expectation that hardens retention economics or reference value; small test mitigates and preserves option value.

mid.rationale: Archive verification reversed the intended direction. Memory_73 shows that while promotional pricing drives +31% signup and +18% qualified revenue, the acquired cohort suffers -12% 30-day retention and fails at renewal—making it net-negative for sustainable long-term qualified revenue despite short-term gains. This directly contradicts the primary objective. Memory_86 confirms that onboarding simplification durably improves both completion and retention (+3% at 30 days), establishing a retention-safe lever. The 6% activation decline and 4% onboarding decline are symptoms of friction in the conversion funnel, not price sensitivity. Activation_messaging (memory_91) lifted week-one engagement and nudged accounts to first meaningful action. Combined with onboarding simplification (memory_86, memory_31), this addresses the root cause—customer struggle, not willingness to pay—while preserving retention economics and long-term value. A standard_experiment tests in-product activation messaging targeted at accounts showing signup completion but low week-one engagement, avoiding the renewal cliff that promotional pricing creates. This protects sustainable revenue while addressing the observed 6% activation decline.

final2.rationale: Context has shifted materially. Churn conversations doubling is an immediate retention crisis that activation_messaging cannot address in the required timeframe. Memory_73 showed promotional pricing causes -12% 30-day retention and renewal failure, but that experiment measured acquisition cohorts entering at discount. Current situation is different: these are *existing customers at risk of switching*. A small_guarded_test of targeted retention pricing on at-risk SMB cohorts is now justified because (1) the counterfactual is losing them entirely to competitor, (2) retention pricing for existing customers has different renewal mechanics than acquisition discounting, (3) small test scope limits downside risk to reference value and pricing precedent, and (4) it buys time for activation_messaging and onboarding simplification to compound their effects. The test must be time-bound and cohort-restricted to prevent generalization of discount expectations. This is a defensive tactical move to stabilize the base while preserving the strategic activation play. Risk is flagged because discount precedent and margin compression are real, but doing nothing in the face of doubled churn conversations is higher risk to sustainable revenue.
